findings.title: Ec2 Imdsv1 Optional
findings.description: The current configuration has http_tokens set to 'optional', which allows IMDSv1 and makes the instance vulnerable to SSRF attacks. By setting http_tokens to 'required', we enforce the use of IMDSv2, which is more secure. This change ensures that the instance metadata service (IMDS) requires a signed token, preventing unauthorized access.
findings.fix_hint: Update the http_tokens value to 'required' to enforce IMDSv2 and prevent SSRF attacks

findings.title: Xentinel Hardcoded Aws Access Key
findings.description: Hardcoding sensitive credentials like AWS access keys and database passwords poses a significant security risk, as they can be exposed to unauthorized parties. Using environment variables to store these credentials helps to keep them secure and separate from the codebase. This approach also makes it easier to manage and rotate credentials without modifying the code.
findings.fix_hint: Use environment variables to store sensitive credentials
findings.fixed_code:
import os
AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID = os.environ.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID')
AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY = os.environ.get('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY')
DB_PASSWORD = os.environ.get('DB_PASSWORD')
STRIPE_SECRET = os.environ.get('STRIPE_SECRET')

findings.title: Xentinel Hardcoded Aws Secret
findings.description: Hardcoding AWS secret access keys poses a significant security risk as it can lead to immediate account takeover. Using environment variables to store sensitive credentials is a more secure approach as it keeps them separate from the codebase. This way, even if the code is exposed, the credentials remain protected.
findings.fix_hint: Use environment variables to store sensitive credentials

findings.title: Tainted Sql String
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to SQL injection because it directly inserts user input into the SQL query. By using a parameterized query, the input is treated as a literal value, preventing an attacker from injecting malicious SQL. This fix ensures that the query is executed safely, regardless of the user input provided.
findings.cwe: CWE-704: Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast
findings.fix_hint: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection vulnerabilities
findings.fixed_code: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"; result = conn.execute(query, (user_id,)).fetchall()

findings.title: Subprocess Injection
findings.description: The original code uses shell=True which can lead to command injection vulnerabilities. By using a list of arguments instead of a string and avoiding shell=True, we can prevent an attacker from injecting malicious commands. The fixed code uses the subprocess module with a list of arguments to safely execute the ping command.
findings.cwe: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Use the subprocess module with a dictionary to allowlist a set of commands and avoid shell=True to prevent command injection vulnerabilities

findings.title: Dangerous Subprocess Use
findings.description: The subprocess function is vulnerable to command injection because it directly executes user-controlled input. Using shlex.escape() will properly escape the input, preventing malicious actors from injecting arbitrary commands. This fix should be applied to the ping function in the provided code snippet.
findings.cwe: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Use the shlex library to escape user-controlled input for the subprocess function

findings.title: Subprocess Shell True
findings.description: The original code uses shell=True, which can lead to command injection attacks. By passing the command and arguments as a list, we avoid the shell and prevent injection. This fix ensures that only the intended ping command is executed, without allowing arbitrary shell commands.
findings.cwe: CWE-78: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Replace the subprocess call with a safer alternative that avoids shell injection

findings.title: Path Traversal Open
findings.description: The vulnerability exists because the filename is directly used to open a file without any validation or sanitization, allowing an attacker to traverse the file system. To fix this, we need to remove any directory traversal characters from the filename and ensure it's within the expected directory. This can be achieved by replacing '../' and '..\' with an empty string and prepending the expected directory path.
findings.cwe: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
findings.fix_hint: Validate and sanitize the filename to prevent path traversal attacks
findings.fixed_code: filename = request.args.get('name'); filename = filename.replace('../', '').replace('..\', ''); filename = '/var/data/' + filename; with open(filename) as f: return f.read()

findings.title: Xentinel Sql Injection Format
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to SQL injection because it directly interpolates user input into the query string. Using parameterized queries with the '?' placeholder and passing the user input as an array to the query method prevents the input from being executed as SQL code. This fix ensures that the input is treated as literal input, not as part of the SQL command.
findings.fix_hint: Use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection
findings.fixed_code: const query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? AND password = ?'; conn.query(query, [username, password], (err, results) => { callback(results && results.length > 0); });

findings.title: Security group allows unrestricted RDP (port 3389)
findings.description: The current security group rule allows unrestricted access to RDP on port 3389, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to restrict the access to only trusted IP addresses or CIDR blocks. By updating the security group rule to include a specific CIDR block, we can prevent unauthorized access to the RDP port.
findings.fix_hint: Restrict the security group rule to only allow RDP access from trusted IP addresses or CIDR blocks
findings.fixed_code: aws_security_group_rule.app_sg_rule { type = "ingress" from_port = 3389 to_port = 3389 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["192.168.1.0/24"] }

findings.title: Security group allows unrestricted SSH (port 22)
findings.description: The current security group rule allows unrestricted access to port 22, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to restrict the source IP address range to a specific IP or subnet. By updating the security group rule to only allow access from a specific IP address, we can significantly reduce the attack surface.
findings.fix_hint: Restrict the security group rule to only allow SSH access from a specific IP address or range

findings.title: RDS instance publicly accessible
findings.description: The RDS instance is currently publicly accessible, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, the 'publicly_accessible' attribute should be set to false to restrict access to the instance. This change will prevent the instance from being accessible over the internet.
findings.fix_hint: Set the 'publicly_accessible' attribute to false for the RDS instance

findings.title: S3 bucket allows public ACL
findings.description: The current configuration allows public access to the S3 bucket, which is a critical security risk. Setting the ACL to private restricts access to only authorized users. This fix should be applied to the aws_s3_bucket resource in the main.tf file.
findings.fix_hint: Set the ACL of the S3 bucket to private to prevent public access

findings.title: S3 bucket allows public ACL
findings.description: TERRAFORM check CKV_AWS_20 failed on resource 'AWS::S3::Bucket.AppBucket'.
findings.fix_hint: Set the ACL of the S3 bucket to private to prevent public access

findings.title: S3 Block Public Access not enabled
findings.description: The S3 Block Public Access feature prevents public access to S3 buckets, which is a critical security control. By enabling this feature, you can prevent unauthorized access to your S3 bucket. This can be achieved by adding the block_public_access configuration to the AppBucket resource in the Terraform configuration.
findings.fix_hint: Enable S3 Block Public Access on the AppBucket resource

findings.title: S3 bucket allows public policy
findings.description: The current S3 bucket policy allows public access, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to update the policy to deny public access to the bucket and its objects. This can be achieved by adding a deny statement to the policy document with a principal of '*' and an action of 's3:*'.
findings.fix_hint: Update the S3 bucket policy to restrict public access

findings.title: IAM policy allows wildcard resource (*)
findings.description: The current IAM policy allows access to all resources using a wildcard (*), which is a security risk. To fix this, the policy should be updated to specify explicit resources, such as the ARN of the specific EC2 instances that require access. This change will help prevent unauthorized access to other resources in the account.
findings.fix_hint: Update the IAM policy to specify explicit resources instead of using a wildcard (*)

findings.title: Admin Managed Policy: AdministratorAccess
findings.description: The current policy grants unrestricted AWS access, violating the principle of least privilege. A custom policy should be created that only grants the necessary permissions for the AppLambdaRole, such as lambda execution and logging. This will prevent unauthorized access and reduce the attack surface.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy that only grants necessary permissions for the AppLambdaRole

findings.title: Dangerous IAM action: iam:*
findings.description: The original policy grants full IAM control, which is a critical security risk. The fixed policy only allows specific required actions, such as passing a role, getting a role, listing roles, and creating a lambda function. This reduces the attack surface and prevents privilege escalation.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the 'iam:*' action with specific required actions in the AppInlinePolicy

findings.title: Privilege Escalation Path Detected
findings.description: The original policy allows the DeployUser to create a Lambda function with any role, which is a privilege escalation path. By specifying the exact role that can be passed, we limit the potential for abuse. This fix restricts the iam:PassRole action to only the app-lambda-role, preventing the creation of Lambda functions with arbitrary admin roles.
findings.fix_hint: Remove the wildcard resource specification for the lambda:CreateFunction and iam:PassRole actions

findings.title: Dangerous IAM action: *
findings.description: The current policy grants all AWS permissions to all resources, which is a critical security risk. To fix this, we need to specify the exact actions required by the lambda function, such as logging permissions. By replacing the wildcard action with a specific set of actions and restricting the resource to a specific ARN, we can significantly reduce the attack surface.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the wildcard action with a specific set of actions required by the lambda function

findings.title: Admin Policy Reference: AdministratorAccess
findings.description: The AdministratorAccess policy grants full AWS access, which is a security risk. A custom policy should be created to grant only the necessary permissions, such as logging, for the lambda execution role. This fix replaces the attachment of the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy that grants only the required permissions.
findings.fix_hint: Replace the AdministratorAccess policy with a custom policy that grants only the necessary permissions for the lambda execution role

findings.title: Aws Db Instance No Logging
findings.description: The RDS instance is missing logging, which can cause important event information to be lost. Enabling logging will allow for better monitoring and debugging of the database instance. The enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports parameter should be set to include the desired log types, such as error-log, general-log, and slowquery-log.
findings.cwe: CWE-311: Missing Encryption of Sensitive Data
findings.fix_hint: Enable logging for the RDS instance by setting the enabled_cloudwatch_logs_exports parameter

findings.title: Rds Insecure Password Storage In Source Code
findings.description: The hardcoded password in the aws_db_instance resource is insecure and should be replaced with a randomly generated password. The random_password resource can be used to generate a random password, which is then passed to the aws_db_instance resource. This ensures that the password is not stored in plain text in the Terraform configuration.
findings.fix_hint: Use the aws_db_instance resource with a random password generated by the random_password resource
findings.fixed_code:
resource "aws_db_instance" "app_db" {
  identifier             = "app-database"
  engine                 = "mysql"
  engine_version         = "8.0"
  instance_class         = "db.t3.micro"
  allocated_storage      = 20
  db_name                = "appdb"
  username               = "admin"
  password               = random_password.app_db_password.result
  publicly_accessible    = true
  skip_final_snapshot    = true
  storage_encrypted      = false
  deletion_protection    = false
}

resource "random_password" "app_db_password" {
  length = 16
  special = true
}

findings.title: Aws Ec2 Has Public Ip
findings.description: The current configuration allows public access to the EC2 instance, which is a security risk. By setting associate_public_ip_address to false, the instance will not be assigned a public IP address, blocking public access. This change will help prevent unauthorized access to the instance.
findings.cwe: CWE-1220: Insufficient Granularity of Access Control
findings.fix_hint: Set associate_public_ip_address to false to prevent public access to the EC2 instance

findings.title: Sql Injection Db Cursor Execute
findings.description: The original code is vulnerable to SQL injection because it directly inserts user input into the query string. Using parameterized queries, as shown in the fixed code, allows the database driver to properly escape the input and prevent injection attacks. This approach ensures that the input is treated as a literal value, rather than part of the SQL code.
findings.cwe: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')
findings.fix_hint: Use parameterized queries or an ORM to prevent SQL injection

findings.title: Avoid_App_Run_With_Bad_Host
findings.description: Running the Flask app with host 0.0.0.0 makes it accessible from any IP address, which is a security risk. Changing the host to 127.0.0.1 restricts access to the local machine only. Additionally, debug mode should be set to False in production to prevent exposure of full stack traces.
findings.cwe: CWE-668: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere
findings.fix_hint: Change the host parameter in the app.run function to a specific IP address or localhost to prevent public exposure

findings.title: Debug Enabled
findings.description: The debug mode in Flask should be disabled in production to prevent sensitive information leakage. Setting debug to False will prevent full stack traces from being exposed. Environment variables can also be used to configure the debug mode for more flexibility.
findings.fix_hint: Set the debug mode to False or configure it using environment variables

findings.title: Direct Response Write
findings.description: The vulnerability occurs because user input is directly interpolated into the HTML response, allowing an attacker to inject malicious scripts. To fix this, use a template engine like EJS or Pug to render HTML and automatically escape user input. This ensures that any user-provided data is properly sanitized and cannot be used for XSS attacks.
findings.cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
findings.fix_hint: Use template engine to render HTML and escape user input

findings.title: Raw Html Format
findings.description: The original code directly interpolates user input into HTML, making it vulnerable to XSS attacks. To fix this, we use DOMPurify to sanitize the user-provided name, preventing any malicious code from being executed. This ensures that only safe and expected content is rendered in the HTML response.
findings.cwe: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')
findings.fix_hint: Use a templating engine or a sanitization library like DOMPurify to prevent XSS vulnerabilities

findings.title: Security group unrestricted ingress
findings.description: The security group 'app_sg' has an unrestricted ingress rule, allowing traffic from any IP address. This is a high-severity vulnerability as it exposes the resource to potential attacks. Restricting ingress to specific IP addresses or security groups mitigates this risk.

findings.fixed_code: resource "aws_security_group" "app_sg" { ingress { from_port = 22 to_port = 22 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["10.0.0.0/16"] } }

attack_chains.title: Cloud Infrastructure Takeover
attack_chains.description: An attacker gains access to the cloud infrastructure by exploiting hardcoded AWS credentials in the code, then uses the unrestricted security group rules to access the EC2 instance and finally escalates privileges using a dangerous IAM policy. This allows them to take full control of the cloud infrastructure and exfiltrate sensitive data.
steps: Step 1: attacker reads hardcoded AWS access key using finding 03fffa79 in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/app.py
Step 2: attacker uses the access key to access the EC2 instance through the unrestricted security group rule finding 8fabedb6 in file uploaded_repo/xentinel-demo-repo/infra/main.tf
Step 3: attacker escalates privileges using the dangerous IAM policy finding 14c1f37c in file xentinel-demo-repo/infra/stack.json
attack_chains.remediation: Remove hardcoded AWS credentials from the code and rotate all access keys

attack_chains.title: Data Exfiltration via SQL Injection
attack_chains.description: An attacker exploits a SQL injection vulnerability in the code to extract sensitive data from the database, then uses the tainted SQL string to execute malicious queries and finally exfiltrates the data using the publicly accessible S3 bucket. This allows them to steal sensitive data without being detected.
steps: Step 1: attacker exploits SQL injection vulnerability using finding f2f7e6d3 in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/auth.js
Step 2: attacker uses the tainted SQL string to execute malicious queries using finding 8bb16cf1 in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/app.py
Step 3: attacker exfiltrates the data using the publicly accessible S3 bucket finding 1fa4b4cb in file uploaded_repo/xentinel-demo-repo/infra/main.tf
attack_chains.remediation: Validate and sanitize all user input to prevent SQL injection attacks

attack_chains.title: Privilege Escalation and Cloud Compromise
attack_chains.description: An attacker exploits a subprocess injection vulnerability in the code to escalate privileges, then uses the escalated privileges to access the cloud infrastructure through the unrestricted security group rules and finally compromises the entire cloud infrastructure using a dangerous IAM policy. This allows them to take full control of the cloud infrastructure and exfiltrate sensitive data.
steps: Step 1: attacker exploits subprocess injection vulnerability using finding 0399035c in file xentinel-demo-repo/src/app.py
Step 2: attacker uses the escalated privileges to access the EC2 instance through the unrestricted security group rule finding 2be8a0bc in file uploaded_repo/xentinel-demo-repo/infra/main.tf
Step 3: attacker compromises the entire cloud infrastructure using the dangerous IAM policy finding 1a65cc00 in file xentinel-demo-repo/infra/stack.json
attack_chains.remediation: Use a secure method to execute subprocesses and restrict access to sensitive resources
